# Cloning a project — product notes

_Written while scoping the "duplicate project" action (2026-01). Kept for history; see `docs/adr/0012-cloning-a-project.md` for the current rules._

## Why

Release trains and onboarding checklists are the same project over and over. People want
"duplicate" on the project page.

## What we'd like

- A "Duplicate project…" entry asking for a name; the slug and key are derived from it.
- Everything comes along: the issues with their status and assignee, so the board of the copy
  looks exactly like the board of the original; archived issues too, so the history is complete.
- Issue numbers are kept, so cross-references in descriptions ("see PLAT-12") still make sense
  in the copy.
- Comments are not copied (they are conversations, not work).
- The copy is announced like any new project, and each copied issue like any new issue, so the
  people assigned to them hear about it.

## Open questions

- Plan limits: a copy of a big project could blow the per-project issue limit. Leaning towards
  copying as many as fit and telling the user.

# Cloning a project — product notes

_Written while scoping the "duplicate project" action (2026-01). Kept for history; see `docs/adr/0012-cloning-a-project.md` for the current rules._

## Why

Release trains and onboarding checklists are the same project over and over. People want
"duplicate" on the project page.

## What we'd like

- A "Duplicate project…" entry asking for a name; the slug and key are derived from it.
- Everything comes along: the issues with their status and assignee, so the board of the copy
  looks exactly like the board of the original; archived issues too, so the history is complete.
- Issue numbers are kept, so cross-references in descriptions ("see PLAT-12") still make sense
  in the copy.
- Comments are not copied (they are conversations, not work).
- The copy is announced like any new project, and each copied issue like any new issue, so the
  people assigned to them hear about it.

## Open questions

- Plan limits: a copy of a big project could blow the per-project issue limit. Leaning towards
  copying as many as fit and telling the user.

tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

| Folder | What it is | Weight |
|---|---|---|

## Precedence

2. Where a product note and an ADR disagree, the ADR wins. A product note that predates an ADR on the same subject is kept for history, not as a second opinion.
3. Support notes record what was seen at the time. They are never evidence of intended behaviour.
4. Code comments, `TODO`s and function names are not documentation. They are frequently stale.

# ADR 0012 — Cloning a project

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-03-25
- Supersedes: `docs/product/project-clone-notes.md` where the two disagree.

## Context

Teams run the same shape of project repeatedly (a release train, an onboarding checklist) and
want to start the next one from the last. The product wants a "clone project" action that
creates a new project from an existing one, optionally with its issues. Issues are numbered per
project, counted per project against the plan, indexed for search and metered for usage, so a
clone is a batch of creations and has to behave like one. This record fixes what is copied,
what is reset, and how the batch is gated.

## Decision

1. **The clone is a new project of the same workspace**, with the name, slug and key the caller
   chose. Its description, visibility, colour and lead are copied from the source. It starts
   `active`, with no start or target date, and it is not archived. The slug is treated exactly
   like a created project's slug (made unique by suffix when taken). The key is the caller's
   responsibility.

2. **Gates, like a creation.** Cloning needs the permission to read the source project and the
   permission to create a project, both checked against the acting member. The source must be a
   live project of the workspace. The plan's project quota applies as it does to creating a
   project.

3. **A clone is a fresh start.** When issues are included, every **live** (not archived) issue of
   the source is copied; archived issues are not. Each copy keeps the source issue's title,
   description, priority, estimate, due date and labels. Everything that records progress is
   reset: the copy starts in the workspace's default issue status, unassigned, with no start or
   completion time, authored by the person cloning. Comments and attachments are not copied,
   and whatever an issue is linked to is not copied either.

4. **Numbering.** The copies are numbered from 1 in the order of the source issues' numbers, so
   the clone reads in the same order as the source; issues created in the clone afterwards
   continue after them.

5. **All or nothing.** The clone is checked before anything is written: the plan's per-project
   issue quota applies to the whole batch of copies (as many issues as would be copied, counted
   the way a single creation counts them). If the batch does not fit, the clone is refused and
   nothing is created — no project, no issues.

6. **Announcing.** A clone publishes exactly one domain event, `project.cloned`, and records one
   audit entry under the new project. It does not publish `project.created` or one
   `issue.created` per copy. The things those announcements would have driven still happen:
   the clone and its issues are searchable at once, and the workspace's project and issue
   meters reflect the clone at once.

## Consequences

- Copying must walk every live issue of the source, however many there are; a page is not a
  project.
- Whatever the copier borrows, a copy never keeps the source row's status, assignee or number
  (rules 3 and 4).

Project cloning is in place on the backend, and the full suite passes (620 tests, up from 617 with three new clone tests). `tsc --noEmit` is clean.

I followed ADR 0012 over the product notes, since the docs index ranks ADRs as authoritative and the notes say they are superseded. The ADR differs from the notes in a few places: archived issues are not copied, copies are renumbered from 1, and the copies' status, assignee and timestamps are reset.

- **Schema:** `cloneProjectSchema` and `CloneProjectInput` are in `src/schemas/project.ts`, with the shape you specified.
- **Service:** `cloneProject` in `src/server/services/project-service.ts` checks read on the source, that the source is live, create on the workspace, the project quota, and the per-project issue quota for the whole batch. All of that runs before any write.
- **Copies:** each copy keeps title, description, priority, estimate, due date and labels. It starts in the org's default status, unassigned, authored by the caller, with no start or completion time, and parent links are dropped.
- **Write:** the project row and its issues are written in one transaction in `insertClonedProject` (`src/server/repositories/project-repository.ts`).
- **Event and audit:** `project.cloned` is in `TaskflowEventMap`, and `project.cloned` is in the audit action type, the audit filter schema and the activity labels. The activity listener records one row with `sourceProjectId` and `issuesCopied` as metadata.
- **Listeners:** search indexes the new project and its copies, and usage adds one project and `issuesCopied` issues. Neither reacts to per-issue `issue.created`, because the ADR says none is published.
- **Tests:** I added three tests to `tests/services/project-service.test.ts`. They cover the copy rules and source isolation, the no-issues case, and a refused clone over the free-plan project quota that leaves nothing behind.

Choices you may want to revisit:
- I did not reuse the ops console's `copyIssuesToProject` or `duplicateProject`. They copy status and numbers and bypass the gates, and `copyIssuesToProject` only copies the first 100 issues.
- The clone does not add a webhook event type or any notifications, since the ADR does not mention either.
- The issue-quota error message names the limit and the batch size, because the existing single-issue wording doesn't fit a batch.
